Title: Key benefits of Zero Trust Network Access over corporate VPN access | Kaspersky official blog
Context: For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device
Full Text:
The tried-and-true recipe for protecting a corporate network has become far less effective than it once was. Guarding the perimeter with a firewall and granting remote access through a VPN gateway has become both cumbersome and risky: day to day, it’s hard to configure how users and cloud services interact, and during cyberattacks the VPN gateway is now a prime target. According to data from insurer At-Bay, nearly three-quarters of the successful ransomware attacks in its 2025 analysis began with a compromised VPN.

To jointly improve network security and operational efficiency, companies need to rethink the remote access model itself. The end goal is a secure connection between an employee and work resources. That by no means implies that an employee (or someone posing as one) should get full access to the corporate network.

What recent VPN attacks show

VPN technology itself isn’t fatally outdated — as long as you treat it as a way to encrypt and tunnel traffic. The problem is how VPN is most commonly deployed: a user authenticates at the entry point, lands on the company network, and from there restrictions (if there are any) depend on segmentation, firewalls, and the protection of individual systems. Inside the network, behind the VPN gateway, a user can reach a wide range of internal services with minimal restrictions. Often, the VPN gateway itself is a privileged device, and successfully compromising it gives attackers many ways to take over the network.

For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device. After gaining root privileges, they used the VPN’s own legitimate service account to query the domain controller and collect passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Before that, vulnerabilities in Check Point and SonicWall gateways were similarly exploited, with the SonicWall attacks carried out by the Akira ransomware operators.

Remote work, VPNs, and stolen data

Today, depending on the country, between 12% and 30% of employees work from home either full or part-time. This shift has significantly increased the number of IT systems that need to be reachable from outside the organizations’ networks — often from personal devices. Personal devices are far more likely than corporate ones to get infected with infostealers. As a result, the black market is flooded with corporate credentials stolen from such computers: it represents 30% of everything initial access brokers (IABs) sell.

Even over a VPN, a strictly segmented network can grant only very limited access. But in practice, exceptions pile up over years of operation: a contractor needs access to a whole subnet, an admin gets “everything, temporarily”, an old application needs a few more ports. These exceptions piled up especially fast during the covid pandemic. As a result, a stolen account often opens the door not to a single service but to the entire infrastructure.

VPN administration overhead

For VPN access to work properly and securely, configuring the VPN gateway alone is usually not enough: you have to set up MFA, device posture checks, network segmentation, and log collection separately. Then you have to make all of it work together. A new employee or application may require changes in several systems at once. Each system works correctly on its own, but the rules drift apart, and figuring out why a certain user has no access turns into a tour of five consoles.

What switching to Zero Trust Network Access changes

First and foremost, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) changes the access model itself and its basic unit of access. Instead of “this user has access rights to this subnet”, a ZTNA system makes decisions like “this user, on this device, in this location, who has passed these levels of verification, can access this specific application”.

Such a decision takes into account a combination of factors (identity, device, and so on) that the policy specifies. The right to work with a ticketing system or a customer database shouldn’t automatically let someone connect to a file server or a domain controller.

Depending on the policies, a ZTNA system can grant access to the needed resource behind the scenes through a combination of methods: a dedicated VPN tunnel to a specific internal server, a reverse connection from a corporate application in a private cloud, and others. A legitimate user doesn’t need to know any of this, but an attacker’s ability to move around the network and attack new services will be severely limited.

Keep in mind that ZTNA is a specific tool — just one part of a broader zero trust architecture. Buying a single product doesn’t mean a company has implemented zero trust.

Benefits of switching from a traditional VPN to ZTNA

A well-implemented ZTNA system primarily reduces the potential damage (the blast radius) if part of the infrastructure or someone’s credentials get compromised; at the same time, deploying it also noticeably decreases an attacker’s room to maneuver.

Reducing the risk of gateway attacks

A VPN gateway usually accepts any connection from the internet. Before verifying the user, the gateway closely analyzes incoming connections, cryptographic messages, and requests to its management and authentication portals. A gateway vulnerability lets an attacker run detailed reconnaissance against the system at this stage and bypass authentication altogether.

Some ZTNA architectures reduce this exposure. An internal connector establishes an outbound connection to a cloud broker on its own. The user connects to the broker separately, and access to the application opens after the necessary checks. In such a system, there’s no need to expose your own gateway for remote access at all.

In a ZTNA architecture with a self-hosted broker, you can’t shift the risk to the ZTNA provider. But a number of ZTNA solutions significantly reduce the attack surface of a self-hosted broker too, for example by using Single Packet Authorization. The broker doesn’t process any requests until it receives a correctly formed encrypted packet, which the client uses to prove its authenticity up front.

Limiting the consequences of compromised credentials and workstations

ZTNA can tie access not only to a password but also to the state of the device: whether the organization manages it, whether its certificate is valid, whether the OS is up to date, whether the security software’s databases are up to date, and whether there are any signs of compromise. What’s more, ZTNA can authenticate the same user differently for different tasks. Does the user just want to read the news on the internal portal, and is the computer they log in from already known about? A password is enough. Is the user logging in to a software repository to change application source code, or opening the budget planning system? Then they’ll have to pass phishing-resistant authentication, for example with a hardware key (such as a YubiKey). If the connection type or other parameters change, the user will even have to re-authenticate.

It’s easy to see how a hypothetical infostealer attack gets more complicated in this scenario. It’s not enough to simply steal a password or a browser session. Trying to use them on a new device will cut the connection.

Here, ZTNA functions partly overlap with what EDR and MDM/EMM agents do on the device. That’s why several vendors bundle these capabilities into a single agent. At the same time, ZTNA limits the consequences of an attack but doesn’t replace endpoint protection. If an attacker uses a remote access Trojan (RAT) rather than an infostealer and directly controls an employee’s device, the ZTNA agent may not be able to tell the attacker’s actions from the employee’s.

Improving observability and detecting anomalies faster

When an employee works from home over a VPN, the firewalls, web filters, and SIEM/XDR often see only shallow network telemetry. That’s why, for example, the actions of the Qilin ransomware operators — who exploited an authentication vulnerability in Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2026-0257) — were hard to tell apart from legitimate employee activity.

ZTNA lets you tie access events to specific identities: users, devices, and applications. Depending on the implementation, SOC teams may get connection logs and, for supported protocols, logs of individual requests to specific applications.

With this level of log detail and the right SIEM rules in place, anomalies quickly catch SOC analysts’ attention.

Simplifying access administration

“Guest” and “temporary” VPN access is a perennial headache for IT and infosec teams. Contractor accounts are created as temporary but stay active for years. In 2026, attackers breached a large European financial institution through this kind of poorly controlled access. ZTNA makes just-in-time (JIT) access possible. A contractor’s support engineer gets access only to the web interface of the one server they need, and that access shuts off automatically after a set time (say, two hours or two days).

Reducing regulatory and insurance risks

Both regulators and the cyber-insurance market are pushing for stricter access management. In April 2026, CISA explicitly named standing contractor VPN access as one of the critical threats to industrial networks. Insurers are also reacting to this trend: organizations with outdated VPN configurations are increasingly hit with rising insurance premiums.

A quick plan for migrating from VPN to ZTNA

Overall, the migration plan looks like this:

Take inventory of your remote access: VPNs, RDP servers, vendor gateways, service accounts, and configured firewall exceptions.

Design and fully document an access structure built around applications and roles instead of the familiar subnets.

Review and, if needed, improve your granular system for identifying users, devices, and applications (identity management), since effective ZTNA depends on it. Enable phishing-resistant MFA, and set up policies for access recovery, posture checks, and session revocation.

Outline an isolated pilot scenario that’s relatively easy to implement but not trivial. For example, start with contractor access to a few applications.

Gradually extend ZTNA to new groups of employees and services.

After each migration stage, disable or significantly restrict the access methods that are no longer needed. For the VPNs that remain, apply strict segmentation and monitoring.

Some legacy applications, industrial systems, and site-to-site connections will still need VPN for a long time to come. The goal isn’t to remove those three letters from your infrastructure at any cost, but to make sure VPN gateways stop being an easy target and an effective launchpad for attacks on your network.

Ransomware

Quarterly trends and highlights

Threat actor disruption

In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments.

In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims.

Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit.

Vulnerabilities and attacks

In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts.

CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups:

CVE-2026-15409/CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom.

CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution.

CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally.

CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity allowed OS commands to run with the privileges of the TeamCity server process by way of an authentication bypass through the agent polling protocol. Command execution at that level could give access to configurations, credentials, CI/CD pipelines, and more.

The most prolific groups

This section highlights the most prolific ransomware gangs by number of victims added to each group’s DLS. Qilin (15.39%) holds first place, as it did last quarter. Qilin is followed by The Gentlemen (7.89%), which was especially active in Q1 but did not make the list in Q2. A notable newcomer on the list is Deadlock (4.46%), a relatively young ransomware family first reported in July 2025.

Attacks on macOS

Quarterly highlights

At the beginning of the third quarter, Jamf researchers discovered a new stealer, PamStealer. What sets it apart is its use of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) to verify the administrator password the user enters.

During the quarter, Socket researchers discovered several supply chain attacks that compromised popular npm, PyPI and Cargo (the Rust package manager) packages. The malicious payloads in these packages targeted macOS systems along with others. For example, on July 11, an infected npm package, jscrambler, was published. Its malicious module was an infostealer written in Rust. The infostealer targeted crypto wallets, secrets from various services and browsers, MCP server configurations, and API keys for AI agents. In August, an attack was detected on the arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec Rust crates; it delivered a Rust backdoor to the victim’s device. In September, malicious versions of the MemTensor npm and PyPI packages were published. They delivered a Go backdoor that targeted secrets, configurations, and API tokens of various services.

In August, Jamf researchers also reported discovering a new backdoor, Overlord. It was distributed as fake Zoom installers and had fairly broad spyware functionality, which is not often seen in macOS backdoors: it could eavesdrop through the microphone, watch the user through the camera, capture the screen, and log keystrokes.

In the third quarter, we discovered an updated version of the MacSync crypto stealer and backdoor with a significantly changed payload delivery method.

Title: Virtualization security: attack layers and misconfiguration impact
Context: An attacker only needs one usable route
Full Text:
Introduction

Incidents in virtual environments can begin with a software vulnerability, human error, a configuration weakness, or several of these factors at once. The investigation is rarely limited to the workload. Hypervisors, container runtimes, management consoles, monitoring platforms, identity systems, virtual networks, datastores, backups, and automation accounts all influence what an attacker can reach.

Kaspersky GERT recently investigated two more ransomware cases on ESXi and Proxmox environments in which weak access controls, insufficient network separation, exposed administrative services, and poor management of privileged credentials contributed to the impact. A monitoring system that could reach the virtualization layer also exposed a reusable root credential. Once the attacker controlled that route, ordinary administrative access was enough to affect several hosts. No VM escape was required.

The incidents show why patching and secure configuration must be managed together. A fully patched hypervisor can still be compromised through a shared password, an overprivileged monitoring account, an open SSH path, or an administrator interface reachable from a general server network. NIST guidance places secure configuration baselines, restricted administrative access, current patches, and monitoring across all layers within the same set of sound security practices.

In this article, we’re going to describe both incidents with additional focus on common unsafe practices that were exploited, leading to compromise, as well as remediation tactics. We’ll also discuss the broader scope of threats targeting virtual environments for a better understanding of possible protection strategies.

The connected system defenders must protect

A business virtual environment is not just Hyper-V, VMware, or Docker but rather a connected stack. Management consoles, orchestration tools, monitoring platforms, and automation accounts sit above hypervisors and container engines. Registries, image stores, virtual switches, datastores, and backup systems connect the layers. Applications and business services run at the bottom, while much of the administrative power sits near the top.

The important boundaries extend beyond guest to host. They include workload to management plane, monitoring system to hypervisor, registry to deployment, administrator workstation to console, management plane to storage, and one virtual network segment to another. An attacker only needs one usable route. The possibility of compromise may lie in one stolen or insecurely placed administrator credential rather than in a complex escape exploit. In the GERT case, the compromise route passed through the monitoring platform and included a valid virtualization platform credential.

Case #1: From network monitoring to ESXi encryption

The investigation began with evidence of BlackNevas ransomware activity on a Windows system in a virtualized domain controller segment. UserAssist artifacts recorded execution of the AnyDesk RMM tool and GMER binaries. The environment also used PRTG Network Monitor to monitor its virtual infrastructure.

UserAssist artifacts

The available evidence showed that the PRTG deployment had broad access to the ESXi hosts and that the same root password was reused across several nodes. After obtaining access to the monitoring environment, the attacker used the ESXi credential to connect over SSH to the hosts that shared the same password. This design joined monitoring, credential storage, and direct administration into one attack path.

PRTG supports storing VMware credentials at the device or inherited group level. That feature is operationally useful, but a monitoring server becomes privileged infrastructure when it holds credentials that can administer the systems it observes. The security question is therefore not whether monitoring needs access, but whether the identity, privileges, storage method, and permitted network path are limited to the monitoring task.

The threat actor gained root access to the ESXi environment and used the esxcli command to bypass the system restriction by disabling the execInstalledOnly policy to execute the encryption binary and also perform anti-forensic log deletion. Let’s look closely at the timeline of the initial host compromise.

ESXi (192.168.*.*) timeline

2025-10-18 Connection attempts from IP address 192.168.*.*. 2025-10-19 During an SSH session by root from IP 192.168.*.*, the file esx is uploaded to the system. 2025-10-19 User "root" attempts to execute the binary esx with the error "Execution of non-installed file prevented". chmod 777 esx ./esx /log 2025-10-19 User "root" deactivates the execInstalledOnly option. esxcli system settings advanced set -o /User/execInstalledOnly -i 0 2025-10-19 User "root" executes the malware esx. 2025-10-19 New connection attempts from IP 192.168.*.*.

Now, at the same time, the following activities ensued on a different host with the same password for the root user:

2025-10-19 SSH connection by user "root" from IP 172.16.*.*. 2025-10-19 User "root" executes the malware esx and clears the logs. chmod a+x esx && chmod 777 esx ./esx /selftest nohup ./esx /p /vmfs/ /depth 5 /log /wipe ./esx /depth 5 /log /wipe

Case #2: Credential notes impacting the whole Proxmox environment

GERT responded to a ransomware incident by The Gentlemen group, in which the threat actor gained access to Proxmox using information collected during the dwell time between initial access and visible impact. On a compromised system administrator workstation, the actor discovered administrative credentials and access details stored in notes in plain text. These records provided the information needed to log in to Proxmox using the root account.

The actor then activated the VNC web socket through the compromised root account, gaining extensive control over the Proxmox environment. This access was subsequently used to download and execute ransomware within the cluster, which resulted in the encryption of the entire virtual environment. Below are the log records showing the root account being used to access other hosts via a VNC web socket.

root@pam [01/08/2026:00:28:36 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=**** root@pam [01/08/2026:00:30:17 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=**** root@pam [01/08/2026:00:31:19 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=**** root@pam [01/08/2026:00:43:38 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=**** root@pam [01/08/2026:00:44:49 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=****

This incident is a clear example of the risks of storing privileged credentials in unsecured notes or other easily accessible files. Once the administrator workstation was compromised, the saved credentials allowed the actor to move from a single endpoint into the virtualization management layer. Because the credentials belonged to a highly privileged root account, one poor credential handling practice significantly increased the scope and impact of the attack. Privileged credentials should instead be stored in an approved password manager or privileged access management system, protected with multifactor authentication and rotated immediately if an administrator workstation is suspected of being compromised.

Why the misconfiguration caused broad impact

Both cases exhibited unsafe misconfiguration practices whose exploitation led to a bigger impact on the host system. Next, we will break down each misconfiguration to see how it enabled further compromise and what should be done to avoid it.

Monitoring inherited excessive privilege

In Case 1, the monitoring platform could do more than collect health and performance data. It held or could use credentials with enough privilege to reach ESXi directly. A compromise of the monitoring system therefore became a compromise of the management plane. Monitoring identities should be dedicated to the task and given only the permissions required by the deployed sensors.

Credential reuse

Password reuse converted one recovered secret into farm-wide access. System administration should use named identities through the central management plane. Each host should have unique credentials and proper password storage hygiene. Password strength alone does not limit the impact of theft, but where the credential can be used and where it is stored do.

Direct root access bypassed central control

Direct SSH access allowed the actor to authenticate as root, upload a binary, and change a security setting without first passing through vCenter role controls. Broadcom, the parent company of VMware, recommends managing vSphere through vCenter, disabling SSH during normal operation, and using Lockdown Mode where suitable. Required service accounts should be explicit exceptions rather than members of a broad administrator group.

Lack of enhanced security settings

The initial execution attempt was blocked by execInstalledOnly, but the attacker had enough privilege to disable this policy. Broadcom documents enforcement options that combine execInstalledOnly with UEFI Secure Boot and TPM-backed configuration protection. These controls must be enabled, tested, and monitored for change. A setting that can be silently disabled by the same credential used for daily administration provides limited resistance after account compromise.

Unsafe credential storage

Case 2 demonstrated the possibility of compromise lying in privileged credential exposure. The mitigation strategy involves not only securing the administrative credential storage but also general hardening practices of secret handling, such as privilege management and regular access audits.

How to close this attack path

In this section, we share remediation advice on how to mitigate such attacks, and detect and prevent them from going further. We recommend the following actions:

Separate monitoring from administration. Create a dedicated monitoring identity for each platform and restrict it to the smallest set of objects and actions that the monitoring sensors require. Do not use ESXi root or another emergency account for routine polling. Prevent monitoring servers from starting interactive administrator sessions unless a separately approved support workflow requires it. The same principle applies beyond VMware.

Replace stored root passwords. Locate every copy of hypervisor, management, storage, and backup credentials in monitoring tools, scripts, scheduled tasks, connection managers, and service configurations. Replace static passwords with vault retrieval, brokered identities, or limited API tokens where the platform supports them. Record every retrieval and rotate the secret after emergency use or compromise.

Restrict direct host access. Route normal ESXi administration through vCenter and enable an appropriate Lockdown Mode after testing monitoring, backup, and recovery dependencies. Keep ESXi Shell and SSH stopped by default. When support work requires SSH, enable it for a defined period, restrict the source, and alert on service activation, root login, and changes to the exception list of users who are allowed to connect via SSH.

Use a specialized security solution. In our portfolio, Kaspersky Cloud Workload Security (KCWS) is perfectly suited to address virtual environment risks, offering a powerful combination of two products: Kaspersky Hybrid Cloud Security (KHCS) and Kaspersky Container Security (KCS). Kaspersky Hybrid Cloud Security is specifically built to secure virtualized infrastructures, private data centers, and hybrid clouds. A patented Light Agent architecture minimizes resource impact without compromising performance, while comprehensive infrastructure visualization through a unified console gives administrators complete visibility and control over the entire hybrid network. Kaspersky Container Security covers every stage of a containerized app’s lifecycle, from development to operation. Among other capabilities, the solution allows for detecting misconfigurations using a dedicated scanner for images, file systems, and repositories that contain IaC files (such as Terraform, CloudFormation, Azure ARM templates, Helm charts, and Dockerfiles).

Treat configuration changes as security events. Alert when execInstalledOnly, Secure Boot enforcement, Lockdown Mode, SSH, local accounts, exception users, firewall rules, or remote logging settings change. Baseline the expected state and test whether the security team can detect an unauthorized change. A secure configuration set once does not mean that the control remains active on the host.

Isolate the management network. Place hypervisor, monitoring, backup, storage, and cluster administration on restricted management networks. Permit only the exact source and destination services required. Administrative workstations should enter through hardened jump hosts with named identities and multifactor authentication.

Protect logs, backups, and recovery. Forward ESXi, vCenter, Proxmox monitoring, identity, and network logs to protected storage that a compromised administrator cannot erase. Backup platforms should use separate identities, restricted management paths, and recovery copies outside ordinary administrative reach.

Configuration checks for monitored virtualization

Below are recommended checks to run when enabling virtualization monitoring. The safest state depends on the platform and monitoring method, but each control should be tested.

Control area

Safer state

Verification

Monitoring identity

Dedicated service account or token with only required read and polling rights

Review assigned roles and test every sensor without root or global administrator access

Credential storage

No recoverable host root password on a monitoring or general-purpose server

Review tool configurations, scripts, scheduled tasks, and connection stores for embedded credentials, access tokens, or other secrets

Test management ports from monitoring server, user segments and untrusted network segments

The wider attack surface

Closing the monitoring and credential routes does not secure the environment by itself. Virtualization also relies on isolation boundaries, trusted images, management APIs, virtual networks, storage, and backups. Each layer requires a different control and leaves evidence in a different place.

VM and container escapes

In a VM escape, code inside a guest reaches past the VM boundary and affects the host or another guest. The weakness may be in a virtual device, an integration feature, a hypercall interface, or another component that translates guest requests for the host. If the escape works, control of one VM may lead to control of the physical server and every workload on it. VMware CVE-2025-22224 showed this risk: an attacker with administrator rights inside a VM could execute code as the VMX process on the host, and Broadcom reported exploitation in the wild.

A container escape can reach a similar result, but the starting point is different. Linux containers share the host kernel, so their isolation model differs from that of a VM. Namespaces limit what processes can see, cgroups control resource use, and capabilities split root privileges into smaller parts. A kernel or runtime bug can break this isolation. Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431) is a good example of a kernel flaw. Code already running in a container could use a Linux AF_ALG crypto socket to change pages in the shared Linux kernel page cache. Because the host and other containers may read the same cached pages, the effect did not have to stay inside one container. The fix is a kernel update; Docker Engine 29.4.3 also tightened its default security profiles to reduce exposure on hosts that had not yet been patched.

Unsafe settings can also break the boundary. Privileged mode, excessive capabilities, writable host mounts, or access to the Docker socket may remove isolation without any software exploit. For instance, runc CVE-2024-21626 involved leaked file descriptors that could expose the host filesystem to a malicious image or container process.

This difference changes the investigation. A VM can often be treated like a separate computer with its own kernel, memory, and disk. A container is a group of host processes placed inside namespaces. If investigators collect only the container filesystem, they may leave the most useful process, socket, and control-plane evidence on the host.

Images and templates

A compromised golden VM image or container base image can spread through normal automation. Common weaknesses include unofficial public images, mutable tags, overprivileged build tokens, recoverable secrets in older layers, and stale templates that restore vulnerable software or forgotten accounts. Scanning might help, but it does not establish who built the artifact or whether the exact image tested and approved was the one ultimately deployed to production. Use controlled builders, provenance records, signature checks, and planned rebuilds from trusted sources.

Management tools and APIs

A stolen vCenter identity, exposed Docker API, overpowered Portainer role, or compromised backup console may give an attacker an easier route than an escape exploit. Portainer advisory GHSA-7fw3-x4r2-g7wc showed how a proxy validated one bind-mount representation but missed an equivalent API form, allowing an authenticated non-administrator with container creation privileges to reach host paths. The runtime performed a valid request after authorization had already failed in the management layer.

Administrative file-copy operations also deserve attention. Docker fixed archive and mount-handling flaws in CVE-2026-41567, CVE-2026-41568, and CVE-2026-42306. These cases required particular conditions and operator or API activity. They are a reminder to patch the daemon and record who initiated copy operations, which container was involved, the source and destination paths, and the result.

Virtual networks, storage, and backups

East-west traffic between virtual workloads may stay inside one host and bypass a physical sensor. Management, migration, storage, and workload traffic should use separate zones with filtering between them. Snapshot and memory files may contain credentials, while weak datastore permissions can expose whole virtual disks. Backup systems need broad access to recover services, which also makes them valuable to an attacker who wants to delete recovery points or reach several hosts.

Attack surface examples by layer

To sum up, the described attack vectors might be mitigated as follows:

Conclusion

GERT cases that we presented in this article did not require an attacker to break the VM boundary. The attack path was created by an overprivileged monitoring relationship, an insecure password storage approach, a recoverable and reused root credential, broad management-network reachability, and direct SSH administration. Each element was legitimate on its own, but together they allowed one compromise to reach virtualization hosts and their workloads.

Misconfiguration should therefore receive the same operational attention as vulnerability management. Teams need to know where privileged credentials exist, which systems can use them, which network paths make them effective, and which logs will show their use. Escape flaws, unsafe images, API weaknesses, virtual network exposure, and attacks on storage or backups remain serious, but closing the known administrative route should come first.

Title: The SOC Files 5: Ghost in the pipeline, or a fileless SharePoint breach by Storm-2603
Context: Executive summary In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote...
Full Text:
Executive summary

In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote code execution through crafted HTTP requests. One of the threat actors deployed ransomware on the target’s systems after successful exploitation. Microsoft attributed this ransomware-related ToolShell activity to Storm-2603, distinguishing it from other actors whose observed activity was primarily focused on credential theft, espionage, and data exfiltration.

In December, our retrospective analysis identified activity consistent with Storm-2603’s TTPs. This activity involved the attacker using the IIS worker process as an in-memory bridge to the customer’s infrastructure, keeping the access and control layer entirely within w3wp.exe without writing anything to disk. Although subsequent post-exploitation activity generated disk artifacts, the bridge used to maintain access remained memory-resident.

Let’s look in more detail at this attack.

The attack chain, from reconnaissance to infrastructure compromise

Intrusion timeline: Strategic latency and exploitation

The intrusion analyzed in this report occurred in two stages, with a temporal gap between initial access and subsequent exploitation activity. The attack timeline was as follows:

Dec 20 – Vulnerability fingerprinting: A single HTTP request targeted a SharePoint administrative endpoint associated with the ToolPane component to determine whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770.

Dec 21-23 – Tactical latency: A three-day period of silence followed the initial probe, separating the vulnerability fingerprinting from subsequent malicious activity and potentially reducing the likelihood of immediate detection.

Dec 24 – High-intensity re-engagement: On Christmas Eve, when security staffing at many companies is reduced, the full RCE chain was executed through the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) on the same endpoint as the initial probe.

Dec 26 – Incident discovery: The three-day gap initially prevented the December 20 probe from being correlated with subsequent malicious activity, marking the event as low priority. Retrospective analysis established that the probe was the initial phase of the subsequent intrusion.

Intrusion timeline

Initial access validation phase

Vulnerability fingerprinting

A vulnerability fingerprinting request on December 20 marked the first observed interaction with the target. The request originated from infrastructure associated with ONYPHE, an internet-scale attack surface discovery and management platform for identifying exposed assets, vulnerabilities, and cyberthreats. Unlike widely used tools such as Shodan and Censys, which merely provide a list of internet-facing assets correlated with the open-source data about known vulnerabilities, ONYPHE actually checks if the target system is vulnerable.

Fingerprinting with ONYPHE

The request characteristics were consistent with ONYPHE’s vulnerability checks, which use active, non-intrusive probes to identify internet-exposed systems vulnerable to specific CVEs. For ToolShell, ONYPHE adopted the approach used by Niels Hofmans (hazcod). Namely, it attempts to inject a harmless marker into the target server to find out if it is vulnerable.

OFFICIAL ONYPHE CVE CHECKER (TOOLSHELL)

This phase served as a validation step against the SharePoint execution surface exposed over HTTP:

The target processed structured requests through the ASP.NET pipeline without rejection.

The request path reached application logic capable of handling serialized input.

No defensive controls interrupted or altered the execution flow at the application boundary.

Approximately 12 minutes later, a second inbound connection originated from infrastructure associated with Pfcloud UG, a provider operating under a bulletproof hosting (BPH) model. Given the timing and the IP’s documented history of scanning and abusive activity, the connection may represent follow-on reconnaissance against the newly identified target. No exploitation was attempted at this stage.

A connection from an IP address belonging to Pfcloud UG BPH

Active exploitation: Santa took your data and left a backdoor

The main malicious activity occurred on December 24. The actor targeted the same SharePoint host with a crafted request from 45.91.94.204 (45.91.92.0/22, ASN 63473, HostHatch, LLC). This resulted in a webshell execution within the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). The payload was not written to disk; rather, it was loaded directly into the ASP.NET runtime and used during subsequent request processing. The implant remained resident for the lifetime of the affected application domain. This runtime state was lost when the application pool was recycled or IIS was restarted.

Attack originated from an SPN node

The IP address 45.91.94.204 is a Safing Privacy Network (SPN) node. SPN routes each connection through a multilayer VPN path with multiple relay nodes that can obscure the originating IP.

SPN promotes itself as a network that offers strong privacy protection for internet traffic. Its infrastructure resembles Tor’s in many ways, but with some differences. It features the following capabilities:

Speed: Near-VPN performance for high-speed data transfer.

Layer 3 support: Supports multiple protocols like TCP, UDP, ICMP (unlike Tor, which only supports TCP).

App-routing: Direct tunneling without a browser.

Multi-identity: Simultaneous exit nodes to bypass IP rate limits.

Fixed-size packets and padding make it harder to analyze its traffic.

It is less common than Tor, and frequently bypasses standard Tor blocklists.

Webshell architecture

The webshell the attackers injected into the w3wp.exe runtime is a multi-module in-memory framework, where execution is orchestrated through the main component (G.cs) and extended via multiple functional units across namespaces.

The implementation follows a modular C# project structure in which each capability is isolated into its own compilation unit and invoked dynamically at runtime.

Webshell components

“G.cs” pipeline control and C2

Pipeline control

The main webshell component is G.cs. It orchestrates the implant’s execution context, lifecycle, C2 and session management.

To ensure persistence within the runtime, G.cs performs the following actions:

Registers a custom VirtualPathProvider using the non-public RegisterVirtualPassProviderInternal method from the ASP.NET HostingEnvironment class so that ASP.NET uses it for virtual-path processing. The provider is automatically added to the chain of registered virtual path providers.

Delegates the provider’s .NET Remoting lifetime policy to the previous provider in the chain, preserving the existing lifetime behavior.

Additionally, to evade defenses and enable the VirtualPathProvider to be registered even if the application in whose AppDomain the webshell is running is precompiled, the module implements the trust control subversion (T1553) technique:

Uses reflection to check if the application is precompiled.

Extracts pointers for internal state fields for the BuildManager class, which manages application compilation, and modifies them at runtime.

Uses reflection once again to force runtime injection.

G.cs uses the GetCacheKey() function as the interception point for the virtual path processing flow. It processes incoming requests to the SharePoint server and checks their headers to filter out requests from the attacker.

The specific User-Agent in the request headers triggers the webshell execution. If the request doesn’t match this condition, the implant remains dormant, making its traffic harder to recognize.

Command and control layer (in-memory transport)

The same core module (G.cs) implements the communication layer.

Instead of relying on external frameworks or standard beacons, it uses a custom binary protocol with XOR-based obfuscation to exchange data with the C2. These communications blend into normal application traffic. The module uses the GetCacheKey() hook to intercept standard HTTP requests. When a specific User-Agent is detected in the request headers, the module parses it, extracts the payload, and establishes a TCP connection to a target host inside the target’s network if needed.

Bidirectional TCP tunnel initialization

G.cs establishes a full-duplex proxy tunnel to support interactive control. It stores active target sockets in memory to pair concurrent HTTP read and write channels.

TCP connections from the C2 server to arbitrary hosts inside the target network are supported for pivoting and lateral movement. The traffic is proxied through the SharePoint host.

Target-to-attacker data channel

Attacker-to-target data channel

As can be seen in the screenshots, the attackers used the suo5 tool to implement traffic proxying. Its authors promote it as a stable forward-proxying tool for scenarios where outbound internet connections are prohibited.

To increase its performance, G.cs manipulates ThreadPool by raising its limits for concurrent operations and maximum timeout.

ThreadPool manipulation

“Prog.cs”: Execution entry point and task dispatcher

Prog.cs is the entry point that receives command-line arguments and passes them to uk/London.cs. The latter acts as the orchestrator, handling command parsing and privilege escalation (via named pipe impersonation). We’ll review it in more detail later. If the “suo5” command is provided, London.cs triggers G.cs to hook into the ASP.NET runtime as a memory shell. Once active, G.cs independently processes incoming web traffic inside the web server memory.

Host interaction modules

The following modules provide direct system interaction capabilities, each implemented as a separate unit. London.cs triggers these modules when it receives a corresponding command from Prog.cs.

“FileDownloader.cs”

The FileDownloader.cs module downloads arbitrary files from external URLs provided by the C2. It stores the downloaded files in the Program Data directory without any user interaction.

“LoggedOnUsers.cs”

This module enumerates logged-on users and identifies their session types (interactive, service, remote). The results are stored in memory. The attackers can retrieve them using the proxy and tunneling capabilities provided by G.cs.

“ProcessList.cs”

This module lists running processes with full paths to the corresponding executables on the disk. The results are stored in memory and the attackers can retrieve them via G.cs.

“NetworkInfo.cs”

This module extracts information about existing network connections, including protocols, local and remote IPs and ports, and connection state. It also enumerates network interfaces and headers. The results are stored in memory and can be retrieved by the attackers via G.cs.

“MSI.cs”

This module silently installs and executes MSI packages previously downloaded by FileDownloader.cs.

“User.cs”

This module creates administrative accounts using the native SAM RPC subsystem (SAMRPCNative namespace) rather than standard command-line tooling. This may indicate an attempt to evade detection and provide the attackers with privileged stealthy access to target systems that persists after the webshell has finished its work.

SAMRPCNative

The SAMRPCNative namespace implements a low-level C# P/Invoke wrapper for the native Windows samlib.dll library, comprising three types: SAMStructs.cs, SAMMethods.cs, and SAMEnums.cs.

“SAMEnums.cs”

Implements structured bitwise lists and constant flags mapping numeric codes to their security meaning in SAM, and translates system status return codes.

“SAMStructs.cs”

Defines native data structures required for P/Invoke memory alignment and for marshalling. It securely formats and aligns data structures.

“SAMMethods.cs”

Contains external API declarations (P/Invoke) imported from samlib.dll to perform actions such as connecting to the SAM server, creating users and opening domains.

This layer is crucial for the attackers because it enables account operations.

Privilege escalation

The uk namespace contains offensive primitives for privilege escalation. To elevate privileges to SYSTEM, it uses a local token impersonation technique via the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC) interface adopted from the EfsPotato tool.

This functionality is implemented in the uk/London class. It creates a malicious named pipe while the EfsrTiny class (a tiny version of the EfsPotato tool) connects to the LSASS.exe RPC server. Then it’s London.RpcThread function calls the EfsRpcEncryptFileSrv function from EfsrTiny with a crafted \\localhost path. This tricks LSASS.exe into connecting back to the attacker’s named pipe. Finally, the London.Exp function uses ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to coerce and impersonate the LSASS.exe token and spawn a new process via CreateProcessAsUser with SYSTEM privileges. As the webshell resides in the IIS worker process, it has the necessary SeImpersonatePrivilege to perform this technique.

The uk namespace also implements a minimal MSRPC client layer by explicitly defining structures such as RPC_CLIENT_INTERFACE and MIDL_STUB_DESC, thereby spoofing an interface stub. This enables direct interaction with the Windows RPC runtime (Rpcrt4.dll) without relying on MIDL-generated stubs or higher-level RPC abstractions. This provides direct control over binding and marshaling that goes beyond the constraints of standard client APIs.

Post-exploitation activity

Shortly after the webshell injection, the infected worker process spawned msiexec.exe to install a remote MSI payload hosted in Supabase cloud storage. The payload was Velociraptor, an open-source digital forensics and incident response tool – namely version 0.73.4.0 vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264 – that the attackers abused for command execution on the target network.

In October 2025, Cisco Talos reported Velociraptor being leveraged by threat actors as a post-compromise execution framework and attributed this activity to Storm-2603. This tool enables arbitrary command execution, and can be used for various purposes. In our case, it was used for persistence, discovery, data collection and payload execution.

The threat actor used Velociraptor to deploy multiple independent tunneling mechanisms, including Zoho Assist-Unattended Support for unauthorized remote access, VS Code CLI tunneling, Cloudflare Tunnel, and a lightweight reverse proxy utility. By doing so, they attempted to maintain access even if some of their tools were detected and deleted. At this stage, they also no longer depended on the IIS worker process lifecycle and ToolShell vulnerability.

EDR-killing attempts

Once the threat actor had access to the target system, they were able to upload a vulnerable driver that is used by many attackers to terminate EDR solutions. We were able to detect the main driver at C:\programdata\rsndispot.sys (054a32d6033b1744dca7f49b2e466ea2). In addition, the adversary used a malicious DLL (2d9ebf9c042f596f435865b40edad928) in a sideloading attack. This DLL was identified as Warlock ransomware’s AV killer. It was possibly intended to kill security solutions using the vulnerable rsndispot.sys driver.

Ransomware deployment attempt

The attackers made attempts to launch ransomware on the compromised system. However, the Proactive Defense Module in Kaspersky Endpoint Security blocked the ransomware process, effectively preventing this activity. The malware DLL we obtained was identified as Warlock ransomware.

What defenders really need to look for

ToolPane deserialization and CLR artifacts

When the attackers tried to access ToolPane, both the dynamically compiled App_Web_toolpane.aspx assembly and the Microsoft.GeneratedCode helper assembly were present within the same application domain.

Both assemblies are used in legitimate scenarios. App_Web_* assemblies are generated during normal ASP.NET page compilation, while Microsoft.GeneratedCode is typically produced by the XmlSerializer during legitimate serialization workflows. However, a request to the ToolPane endpoint that results in immediate loading of Microsoft.GeneratedCode within the same execution window indicates that the runtime is processing serialized data supplied through the request.

Detecting deserialization exploitation

First, it is highly recommended to read this article (in Russian) on how deserialization exploit attempts in the CLR should be detected, with examples of YARA rules and monitoring recommendations. A summary of the main idea of the detection logic is provided below.

Deserialization vulnerabilities should be treated as a distinct class of exploitation events. In the CLR, deserialization is not merely the conversion of bytes into values – it is the reconstruction of an object graph from an incoming stream. Serialization and deserialization are performed by formatters. One of the most widely used formatters is BinaryFormatter. It uses the NRBF format, which defines the stream as a sequence of records describing classes, arrays, primitives, and references between objects. The shape of the resulting graph is determined by the data supplied to the deserializer. This means that the input stream defines not only the values but also the specific types, relationships, and lifecycle points that the runtime must materialize.

Microsoft states explicitly that BinaryFormatter is unsafe and cannot be made safe; beginning with .NET 9, the in-box implementation is effectively removed from ordinary use. However, Microsoft continues to use it in its products, including SharePoint, because it is powerful and easy to use. To fix BinaryFormatter-related issues, architectural changes are needed. Similar warnings also apply to related unsafe mechanisms, including LosFormatter (used in the vulnerable page).

The primary risk of unsafe deserialization is that the CLR may resolve unexpected types, instantiate objects outside normal constructor invariants, and invoke special lifecycle mechanisms such as ISerializable, IObjectReference, IDeserializationCallback, and methods marked [OnDeserialized]. In other words, the attacker-controlled data can force the runtime to construct a graph containing types with executable side effects.

A practical detection strategy should therefore focus on graph-construction artifacts. CLR loader events identify the relevant assemblies and application domains. Memory and metadata inspection then reveal the type names and generated serializer structures associated with the suspected gadget chain. In ToolShell-like scenarios, unsafe deserialization usually produces helper assemblies (evidence in loader events) with metadata containing fully qualified type names, gadget class names, and string representations of the constructed generic types (just scan via YARA for it). In our case, the artifacts to look for include Microsoft.GeneratedCode, App_Web_toolpane.aspx* (evidence of deserialization in loader events) as well as strings identifying ObjectDataProvider, ExpandedWrapper, and LosFormatter (evidence that the input stream was deserialized into dangerous objects). Note that these indicators are not significant in isolation; their value lies in the fact that they show the runtime has already received data requiring helper code generation to reconstruct a dangerous object graph.

Gadget objects that exploit vulnerabilities like those associated with ToolShell are conveniently represented in corpus-style tooling such as ysoserial.net/YSoNet, which aggregate known gadget chains for unsafe .NET deserialization. For defensive purposes, the value of these projects lies not in their offensive capability but in the catalog of types and structures that can be searched for in streams, memory, and helper assemblies. The presence of any of them in memory or in a helper assembly should be treated as a strong indicator of exploitation.

To simplify deserialization exploit detection, we created a tool named CLRDeserializationExploitFinder. It can detect ToolShell exploitation attempts, as well as other gadget chains covered by ysoserial.net.

Detecting a VPP-based webshell/runtime implant

A mechanism based on VirtualPathProvider should be treated as a separate class of runtime implant (no files involved). In ASP.NET, HostingEnvironment.RegisterVirtualPathProvider registers a new virtual-path provider (VPP) in the application’s compilation system. Once registered, the application can serve virtual paths during dynamic compilation as though they were ordinary on-disk pages. Dynamic compilation does not require the payload to exist as a file in the filesystem. It operates entirely within the trust boundary of the application itself. During the compilation process, temporary files may be generated, but they cannot be treated as reliable forensic artifacts. Because VPPs can also be used for legitimate purposes, the defensive model should begin with an inventory of the legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations. In all other cases, the registration or use of a new VPP should be considered anomalous.

To see how the dynamic generation of virtual pages using ASP.NET, IIS, and the CLR works, and to learn how to detect such activity, use our project VirtualPathProvider Lab.

The most useful telemetry source for this technique is the Microsoft-Windows-IIS-Configuration ETW provider. To detect virtual paths, events 25 and 47 are of primary value. Event 25 records the mapping of ConfigPath to PhysicalPath, and event 47 records the mapping of the configuration path to a directory. In the case of a VPP-backed path, these events create an inconsistency: IIS and ASP.NET behave as if the path has a physical representation, while the corresponding file does not exist on disk. In the example provided by VirtualPathProvider Lab, this appears as a mapping of the virtual resource googlecheck.aspx to a physical path where no real file is present. This discrepancy between configuration resolution and filesystem reality is the primary indicator of virtual content.

The second indicator is more negative than positive. For disk-backed files, IIS normally creates a FileChangeNotificationMonitor chain, as reflected in events 17, 18, 19, and 21. For virtual paths served by a custom VirtualPathProvider, this chain is absent or does not match the normal profile of an ordinary file because there is no physical object or corresponding on-disk change lifecycle. Consequently, the presence of positive events 25 and 47 combined with the absence of the expected events 17, 18, 19, and 21 for the same path forms a reliable detection pattern: the path exists for IIS as a configuration-resolved resource, yet it is not backed by the filesystem and is not accompanied by normal file-change monitoring.

To sum up, the hunting target here is the discrepancy between how IIS/ASP.NET resolves a resource and what is actually present on the disk and in the change-monitoring chain. For known applications, such cases can be filtered through an allowlist of legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations. Anything else should be treated as a potential runtime implant and examined using ETW, filesystem verification, and memory inspection of the w3wp.exe process.

Attribution

Microsoft tracks Storm-2603 as a standalone threat actor with no known links to other groups. While they are careful about assessing the actor’s motivation, they mention that it has previously deployed Warlock and LockBit ransomware following active exploitation of on-premises SharePoint vulnerabilities. In the analyzed incident, we observed similar SharePoint exploitation activities, as well as an EDR killer associated with Warlock ransomware and unsuccessful Warlock launch attempts.

Other documented intrusions have identified Storm-2603 as leveraging known flaws within perimeter mail gateways to achieve initial access, subsequently staging the Velociraptor framework with elevated privileges and establishing persistent encrypted tunnels via commercial remote management software to orchestrate secondary lateral movement. This aligns with the post-exploitation behavior we observed in our case. Together with the ToolShell exploitation scenario, this allows us to attribute this case to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence.

Conclusion

From the incident analyzed in this article, the main defensive lesson is that exploiting an internet-facing SharePoint server can enable fileless code execution directly inside the application trust boundary. Storm-2603 did not require a conventional dropper, persistent service, or exposed C2 endpoint; instead, it deployed a webshell inside w3wp.exe, from which tunneling, privilege escalation, credential access, and lateral movement could be orchestrated. Detection therefore needs to move beyond file-based webshell hunting toward runtime behavior, such as anomalous w3wp.exe activity, unexpected outbound connections, RPC coercion, token impersonation, and the introduction of remote-management or DFIR tooling after application compromise.

To correctly attribute malicious activity and develop appropriate response measures, defenders should reconstruct execution chains and temporal relationships across application, host, and identity layers. They should also preserve memory and IIS telemetry, and correlate low-signal reconnaissance with subsequent privileged activity rather than evaluating events in isolation. A confirmed SharePoint exploit with code execution should trigger host-level containment, persistence hunting, credential and exposed MachineKey rotation, and TTP-driven investigation rather than remediation limited to the initial exploit or known IOCs.
